stories.title: Battle over Allapattah: Miami sues county over neighborhood community redevelopment agency
stories.excerpt: Miami has taken Miami-Dade County to court in a dispute over plans to create a new government agency to bolster growth and redevelopment of the Allapattah neighborhood.  The city of Miami argues in its complaint that the county lost its ability to block or delay the proposed Allapattah CRA by failing to act on the city’s request within a state-mandated deadline under the Florida Community Redevelopment Act, the South Florida Business Journal reported. CRAs, or community redevelopment agencies, allow cities to reinvest new property tax revenue from neighborhoods back into the same areas, including for infrastructure improvements and to spur […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Miami sues Miami-Dade County over Allapattah CRA authorization; city claims automatic approval after 120-day deadline.
Planned $243M redevelopment investment in Allapattah neighborhood over 30 years signals major infrastructure/growth push.
CRA dispute resolution will unlock tax-increment financing and reinvestment authority critical to neighborhood stabilization.
stories.summary: Miami is suing Miami-Dade County to enforce automatic authorization of a Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) for the Allapattah neighborhood after the county failed to respond within the state-mandated 120-day window. The city's redevelopment plan calls for $243 million in targeted investments over 30 years. CRAs allow municipalities to reinvest incremental property tax revenue back into designated areas for infrastructure and growth catalysts.
stories.impact: If Miami prevails, the Allapattah CRA unlocks dedicated tax-increment financing and policy tools that will drive neighborhood stabilization, infrastructure upgrades, and anchor investment—creating a window for multifamily developers to acquire and build ahead of rising valuations and demand in this emerging submarket. The CRA framework also de-risks early-phase development by guaranteeing public reinvestment and improved area fundamentals.

stories.title: First rental complex on tap in burgeoning South Florida city after $13M land deal
stories.excerpt: South Florida’s youngest city is poised to get its first apartment complex, following a $12.6 million deal for an 18-acre site.  Minto Communities USA, the master developer of 10-year-old Westlake, sold the parcel to Eastwind Development, which plans a 360-unit community in eight buildings, according to Minto’s news release. The site is between Town Center Parkway North and South, east of Seminole Pratt Whitney Road and west of Kingfisher Boulevard. It’s across from the Westlake Adventure Park.    The $12.6 million price was confirmed in public records and by real estate database Vizzda. It breaks down to $700,000 per acre.  The […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Eastwind Development pays $12.6M ($700K/acre) for 18-acre Westlake site; first rental complex in 10-year-old city.
360-unit Avery at Westlake approved August 2024; eight buildings (six four-story, two three-story) with family-friendly mix.
Westlake (incorporated 2016) positioned as self-sustaining suburban hub west of Palm Beach County, reducing commute to eastern employment centers.
stories.summary: Eastwind Development acquired an 18-acre parcel in Westlake, Florida for $12.6 million to build Avery at Westlake, a 360-unit community representing the city's first apartment complex. The project, approved by city council in August, includes six four-story and two three-story buildings with one-, two-, and three-bedroom units, plus resort-style amenities. Westlake was incorporated in 2016 as a master-planned suburban community in far western Palm Beach County designed to reduce eastbound commute pressure.
stories.impact: Westlake's approval of its first rental community signals demographic and job-growth maturation in exurban Palm Beach County; this greenfield entitlement and $700K/acre basis suggest strong pre-leasing demand and investor confidence in westward population/employment shift. Developers should monitor Westlake and similar inland Palm Beach submarket opportunities for multi-phase, build-to-suit potential as congestion and land scarcity near I-95 corridor intensify.

stories.title: Bohannon plots mixed-use campus next to Hillsdale mall redevelopment
stories.excerpt: Bohannon Development Company is looking to add office and residential buildings to its development plans for San Mateo’s Hillsdale neighborhood.  Bohannon submitted preliminary plans for a 10-story office tower and a 94-unit affordable apartment building at 3025 South El Camino Real in San Mateo, the Silicon Valley Business Journal reported. The $300 million proposal would raze a former T.G.I. Fridays and accompanying vacant parking lot next to the Hillsdale Caltrain station.  The development, dubbed Platform 31 after its location on the corner of 31st Avenue, would add offices and housing across the street from Hillsdale Shopping Center. Bohannon is also […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Bohannon Development files $300M mixed-use plan: 10-story office tower + 94 affordable units next to Hillsdale Caltrain station.
Platform 31 razed former T.G.I. Friday's; sits across from Hillsdale Shopping Center redevelopment and Roblox HQ expansion (325K SF).
94 apartments restricted to 60% AMI (~$88,260/person); half two- and three-bedroom family units; connects Hillsdale to Bay Meadows office campus.
stories.summary: Bohannon Development submitted preliminary plans for Platform 31, a $300 million mixed-use campus in San Mateo's Hillsdale neighborhood featuring a 10-story office tower, a 94-unit affordable apartment building (60% AMI), and ground-floor retail. The development, on a former T.G.I. Friday's site adjacent to Hillsdale Caltrain station, is designed to create a 'center of gravity' connecting the Hillsdale Shopping Center redevelopment to the Bay Meadows office campus, where Roblox recently leased 325,000 SF for headquarters expansion.
stories.impact: Roblox's major Peninsula HQ expansion signals office recovery and job growth in Silicon Valley's mid-market, driving demand for workforce housing near transit. The adjacency to Caltrain and integration with Bay Meadows office recovery creates rental demand tailwinds for the 94 affordable units, while the mixed-use format reduces single-asset risk and improves financing. Developers should track similar transit-oriented development (TOD) opportunities in Peninsula submarkets where office relocations and tech hiring are accelerating post-pandemic.

stories.title: FPA Multifamily Picks Up 599-Unit MF Community in Portland
stories.excerpt: FPA Multifamily purchased Wimbledon Square and Gardens, a 599-unit residential community in Portland, OR. The property is located at 2837 SE Colt Drive, on over 14 acres. Constructed in phases in 1973 and 1975, Wimbledon Square and Gardens comprises 83 three-story residential buildings offering studio, one-, and two-bedroom apartments and townhomes. Community amenities include three outdoor heated swimming pools with sundecks, a clubhouse, and tennis, basketball, and volleyball courts. The property is adjacent to the Reed College campus and near D.A. Grout Elementary School and Cleveland High School. The nearby SE 17th Avenue and Holgate Boulevard MAX Light Rail Orange Line station provides direct access to Oregon Health & Science University, one of the region’s major employers. The surrounding neighborhoods of Sellwood, Woodstock, Division, and Hawthorne offer easy access to numerous restaurants, retail shops, grocery stores, farmers markets, parks and trails. The property is also near Downtown Portland. Anthony Palladino, Philip Assouad, Giovanni Napoli, Ryan Harmon, and Nick Ruggiero of IPA, in association with David Tabata, Marcus & Millichap’s broker of record in Oregon, represented the seller and procured the buyer in the transaction. The post FPA Multifamily Picks Up 599-Unit MF Community in Portland appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: FPA Multifamily acquires Wimbledon Square and Gardens (599 units) in Portland, OR for undisclosed price.
1973–1975 vintage, 14+ acres, 83 three-story buildings; adjacent Reed College, near OHSU light rail (Orange Line).
Asset positioned near major employer (OHSU) and established neighborhoods (Sellwood, Division, Hawthorne); pool amenities, strong transit access.
stories.summary: FPA Multifamily purchased Wimbledon Square and Gardens, a 599-unit community built in phases (1973–1975) on over 14 acres in Portland. The property comprises 83 three-story buildings with studios and one- and two-bedroom units. The location is adjacent to Reed College, near the SE 17th Avenue/Holgate Boulevard MAX Light Rail Orange Line station providing direct access to Oregon Health & Science University, a major regional employer, and neighboring trendy residential districts.
stories.impact: Portland's acquisition market remains active despite broader multifamily headwinds; OHSU employment stability and MAX transit access support rent growth and occupancy resilience. Dated 1970s product stock and aging amenities suggest value-add opportunity through targeted renovations and operational improvements. The scale and location near a major institutional employer provide defensive income characteristics—relevant for core-plus investors seeking Portland exposure with lower construction and regulatory risk than development-stage assets.

stories.title: Ascendant Capital Partners Acquiring the Westin Seattle Hotel
stories.excerpt: Los Angeles-based Ascendant Capital Partners is acquiring the 891-room Westin Seattle from Host Hotels & Resorts, with HEI Hotels and Resorts slated to take over hotel operations starting January 26, 2027. News of the trade surfaced publicly in a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) filing, indicating that the hotel’s 423 employees would soon be working for a new operator. A sale price has not been publicly announced, as of this report. The two-tower property, located at 1900 Fifth Ave., ranks as the Seattle region’s third-largest hotel by room count. The hotel’s 40-story South Tower opened in June 1969, while the 47-story North Tower opened in June 1982. Built on the former Orpheum Theatre site, the hotel was designed by John Graham & Associates. Amenities include a heated indoor pool, fitness studio with Peloton bikes, dining options such as 1900 FIFTH Bar + Lounge, meeting spaces, valet/private parking, pet-friendly policies, and 51 ADA-accessible rooms. The post Ascendant Capital Partners Acquiring the Westin Seattle Hotel appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Ascendant Capital Partners (Los Angeles) acquiring 891-room Westin Seattle from Host Hotels & Resorts; HEI Hotels taking operations Jan. 26, 2027.
WARN filing signals 423 employee transition; sale price undisclosed; property is Seattle region's third-largest hotel (two towers, 1969 & 1982).
Hotel conversion trend underway; no multifamily demand signal in story.
stories.summary: Ascendant Capital Partners is acquiring the 891-room Westin Seattle from Host Hotels & Resorts, with HEI Hotels and Resorts set to assume operations starting January 26, 2027. A WARN filing disclosed the transition of 423 employees to the new operator. The property ranks as the third-largest hotel by room count in the Seattle region and comprises two towers opened in 1969 and 1982.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily development impact; hotel asset transaction with operational flag for employment transition. Mention of hotel-to-residential conversion trends nationally is worth monitoring in Seattle, where downtown office recovery remains tepid and adaptive reuse of underutilized hospitality stock could yield conversion pipeline—but this deal does not signal conversion intent.

stories.title: Newly Repositioned Park 53 Adds Three to Tenant Roster
stories.excerpt: JLL recently arranged three new office leases totaling 19,145 square feet at Park 53, a newly repositioned boutique office building located at 45 E. 53rd St. in Manhattan’s Plaza District. The JLL agency leasing team representing ownership includes Mitchell Konsker, Benjamin Bass, Alexander Chudnoff, Greg Wang and Thomas Swartz. The transactions include: ● Forest Avenue Capital leased 7,145 square feet. Sinclair Li and Pat Moroney of CBRE represented the tenant. ● Ancient Financial leased 6,000 square feet, represented by Brent Ozarowski and Kevin Sullivan of Newmark. ● Curbline Properties leased 6,000 square feet, represented by Conor Kenny of CBRE. The three firms join an established roster of tenants that includes Acres Capital, Shorenstein and Bramshill Investments. “The Park Avenue corridor continues to attract firms that place a premium on location and the quality of their office environment,” said Konsker. “The activity we’re seeing at Park 53 reflects that demand.” The post Newly Repositioned Park 53 Adds Three to Tenant Roster appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JLL arranged three office leases (19,145 SF total) at Park 53, 45 E. 53rd St., Manhattan Plaza District.
Tenants: Forest Avenue Capital (7,145 SF), Ancient Financial (6,000 SF), Curbline Properties (6,000 SF); established anchor roster includes Shorenstein.
No multifamily development signal; office leasing activity only.
stories.summary: JLL brokered three new office leases totaling 19,145 square feet at Park 53, a recently repositioned boutique building in Manhattan's Plaza District. Tenants include Forest Avenue Capital, Ancient Financial, and Curbline Properties. The property's existing roster includes established firms such as Acres Capital and Shorenstein.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. Office leasing momentum in Manhattan's Plaza District reflects modest midtown office recovery but does not drive residential demand signals or inform apartment development strategy in New York.

stories.title: Vacant Since 2012 Fire, East Flatbush Site Will Yield 134 New Apartments
stories.excerpt: MSquared and project partners broke ground on the redevelopment of 665 New York Ave. in Brooklyn’s East Flatbush neighborhood. The project will bring 134 homes back to a site that has been vacant since a fire in 2012. The project marks the first use of the Mamdani administration’s Subordinate Market Rate Revolving Term Loan, a new public financing tool included in the administration’s housing plan. The loan is designed to return revenue from financed projects to the city, creating a revolving source of public investment that can be reinvested in future affordable housing development. When complete, the mixed-income development will include 90 affordable apartments, including 18 apartments for formerly displaced tenants and 14 homes for formerly homeless New Yorkers. The all-electric building will replace the gas system that served the property before the fire and include parking, bike storage, a rooftop deck and a fitness center. Construction is expected to be complete in 2028. The post Vacant Since 2012 Fire, East Flatbush Site Will Yield 134 New Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MSquared breaks ground on 665 New York Ave., East Flatbush, Brooklyn: 134-unit redevelopment vacant since 2012 fire.
90 affordable units (67%), including 18 for displaced former residents + 14 for formerly homeless; mixed-income model; completion 2028.
First use of NYC Mamdani administration's Subordinate Market Rate Revolving Term Loan; all-electric, rooftop deck, fitness center.
stories.summary: MSquared and project partners broke ground on the redevelopment of 665 New York Ave. in Brooklyn's East Flatbush, bringing 134 apartments to a site vacant since a 2012 fire. The mixed-income project includes 90 affordable units (67% of total), with 18 reserved for formerly displaced tenants and 14 for formerly homeless individuals. The project is the first to use the Mamdani administration's Subordinate Market Rate Revolving Term Loan, a new public financing mechanism designed to generate recurring revenue for affordable housing reinvestment.
stories.impact: NYC's new revolving loan program reduces developer equity burden and de-risks affordable production, signaling scaled capital availability for E. Flatbush and similar underutilized/vacant sites. The displaced-resident and formerly homeless set-asides demonstrate community stabilization focus; this may attract additional public subsidy and community goodwill, lowering predevelopment and entitlement risk. Developers should monitor this new financing mechanism for replicability across other NYC neighborhoods and potential to accelerate brownfield-to-housing pipelines.

stories.title: Hudson County Luxury Multifamily Trades for $46M
stories.excerpt: CBRE announced the sale of The Station, a 97-unit luxury multifamily high-rise property located at 4901 Bergenline Ave. in West New York, NJ, adjacent to the Bergenline Avenue Light Rail Station. The property was sold for $45.6 million, or $470,000 per unit The CBRE team of Fahri Ozturk, Richard Gatto and Zach McHale, along with Jeffrey Babikian, led the marketing campaign and served as exclusive advisors to the seller, AIRN Management. The CBRE team also procured the purchaser. The sale marks the seventh transaction completed on behalf of AIRN Management by CBRE. “The Station represents one of the highest-quality multifamily assets in Hudson County, combining luxury residential units, durable retail income and exceptional transit accessibility,” said Ozturk. “The property’s strong fundamentals and strategic location within one of Northern New Jersey’s most dynamic rental markets generated significant investor interest throughout the marketing process.” Built in 2023, The Station features market-rate residences and approximately 11,000 square feet of retail space on the ground floor. The retail space is fully leased to a regional grocery operator on a long-term basis. The post Hudson County Luxury Multifamily Trades for $46M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CBRE closes sale of The Station (97-unit luxury high-rise) West New York, NJ for $45.6M ($470K/unit).
Built 2023, adjacent Bergenline Avenue Light Rail Station; 11,000 SF retail (fully leased to regional grocer long-term); seven CBRE transactions for AIRN Management.
Hudson County luxury multifamily market remains active; strong transit-oriented valuation.
stories.summary: CBRE completed the sale of The Station, a 97-unit luxury multifamily high-rise in West New York, NJ for $45.6 million ($470,000 per unit). Built in 2023, the property is located adjacent to the Bergenline Avenue Light Rail Station and includes approximately 11,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, fully leased to a regional grocery operator on a long-term lease. The transaction represents the seventh CBRE-brokered deal for seller AIRN Management.
stories.impact: Hudson County's $470K/unit pricing for newer luxury transit-oriented multifamily affirms strong rent growth and investor appetite in Northern New Jersey rail corridor. Light rail adjacency commands premium valuation; developers should prioritize TOD sites along PATH, NJ Transit, and regional light rail networks. The retail-anchored model (grocery co-tenant, long-term lease) reduces residential revenue concentration and improves refinancing profile—relevant for future West New York/Hudson County development underwriting.

stories.title: Key International wants to replace South Beach hotel with residences as luxury condo boom takes off
stories.excerpt: Key International wants to trade oceanfront hotel rooms for luxury condo units in Miami Beach’s South of Fifth neighborhood. The developer, who built the hotel in 2000 and still owns the property, filed plans with Miami Beach’s Historic Preservation Board to demolish the 226-room, 10-story Marriott Stanton Hotel with a 27-unit, 120-story condo tower spanning nearly 300,000 square feet. The adjacent two-story historic Stanton building would remain as a retail property.  Designed by Seattle-based architecture firm Olson Kundig, The Stanton Residences calls for units ranging from 4,290 square feet to 5,300 square feet, with three penthouses featuring private terraces with […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Key International (developer/owner since 2000) seeks to demolish 226-room, 10-story Marriott Stanton Hotel, Miami Beach South of Fifth.
Replacement: 27-unit, 120-story luxury condo tower (~300K SF); units 4,290–5,300 SF + three penthouses; requests 8-foot terraces (vs. 5-foot allowed).
South Beach luxury condo boom underway; hotel-to-condo conversion signals shift from travel to wealth-storage demand.
stories.summary: Key International filed plans with Miami Beach's Historic Preservation Board to demolish the 226-room Marriott Stanton Hotel (built 2000) in the South of Fifth neighborhood and replace it with The Stanton Residences, a 27-unit, 120-story luxury condo tower designed by Olson Kundig. Units range from 4,290 to 5,300 square feet, with three penthouses featuring private terraces and plunge pools. The developer is seeking a variance to allow 8-foot balconies on the northern side (5 feet allowed by right) to maximize unit terraces given setback constraints.
stories.impact: Hotel-to-condo conversion in South Beach reflects wealth migration and luxury housing demand outpacing travel recovery in Miami; signals developer capital reallocation from hospitality to residential. The ultra-luxury (27 units, 4K+ SF average) positioning targets international capital and second-home buyers rather than primary renters—different from traditional multifamily but indicates strong price appreciation expectations and low financing risk in Miami Beach submarket. Monitor similar conversions for signals of market maturation and possible rental softening in lower-tier segments.

stories.title: Nithya Raman Inherits a Downtown L.A. Still Searching for Its Comeback
stories.excerpt: “Downtown L.A. needs attention and it needs real care,” said Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman during a May debate. “It needs a strategy.” In the run-up to the election, she said, “Everything about the future of Los Angeles is currently being bet on Downtown L.A.” Raman will enter office Dec. 13 as the Downtown L.A. market enters a crucial turning point. Years of being “one of the deadest downtowns in the world,” per a Los Angeles Times headline earlier this year, have started to show signs of shifting. The so-called “Graffiti Towers” have been scoured and shorn of spray paint, and the continued departure of office tenants reversed in the third quarter, as increased signing of modest leases, including tenants at the U.S. Bank Tower, meant more office space being filled than vacated. The market overall saw 85,000 square feet in net absorption. Apartment occupancy downtown hit 91.4 percent, its highest level in the last three years. Workers continuing the removal of the remaining graffiti from Oceanwide Plaza, also known as the “Graffiti Towers,” in Downtown Los Angeles on November 12. The extensive cleanup has dramatically transformed the appearance of the three-tower development. photo: Los Angeles Times via Getty Images “The last year has marked a huge shift in downtown progress,” said Nella McOsker, president and CEO of Central City Association of Los Angeles (CCA). “You’re seeing the tides turn. But there’s still a long way to go.” And with a number of high-profile developments and events coming in the next 18 months — the $2.6 billion expansion of the downtown convention center, the hoped-for redevelopment of Oceanwide Plaza, the beginning buildout of the Fourth & Central megadevelopment, and the Olympics and the media attention it will bring — this may be a unique moment to revitalize the oft-maligned neighborhood. During the summer games, downtown will be a primary hub. Advocates for downtown believe Raman has an innate respect for the impor
bullets: LA Mayor-elect Nithya Raman takes office Dec. 13; prioritizes downtown revival; describes DTLA as 'one of deadest downtowns in world.'
Downtown LA shows early stabilization: office net absorption positive Q3 2024 (85,000 SF); 'Graffiti Towers' cleaned; office departures reversed.
Long way to go; market at 'crucial turning point' with renewed landlord/developer focus on mixed-use, housing, and street-level activation.
stories.summary: Incoming Los Angeles Mayor Nithya Raman takes office December 13, 2024, with downtown Los Angeles revival as a central priority. After years of severe decline, early stabilization signals have emerged: office net absorption turned positive in Q3 2024 (85,000 SF), departures slowed, and aesthetic improvements (e.g., graffiti removal) are underway. CCA president noted the market has reached an inflection point, though substantial challenges remain.
stories.impact: DTLA's shift from distressed to stabilizing opens a medium-term window for mixed-use and adaptive-reuse multifamily development; leadership focus and modest office recovery reduce regulatory and market timing risk. Early office absorption reversal (even modest) signals employer confidence returning; this supports workforce-housing demand and mixed-use projects with ground-floor retail/office. Developers should track Raman's housing and incentive policies, vacancy rate trends, and office pre-leasing momentum—a 2–3 year window likely exists before DTLA valuations and cost-to-build compress opportunities.

stories.title: New West Palm Beach Condo Lands $57M Loan With Nearly Half Its Units Unsold
stories.excerpt: Is the market for new-construction condos in West Palm Beach finally slowing? BGI Companies and Blue Road nabbed a $56.5 million loan for a newly completed waterfront condo development in the South Florida city. The condo inventory loan from Kriss Capital backs 22 units — or nearly half of the total — that remain unsold within the Alba Palm Beach project, according to public mortgage documents. The 55-unit condo building at 4714 North Flagler Drive faces the Intracoastal Waterway, about three miles north of West Palm Beach’s downtown. “This is a customary refinancing process for a condominium project at this stage,” BGI Companies co-founder Kenneth Baboun said in a statement shared with Commercial Obsercer. “We continue to see strong interest in the remaining residences currently available and are very pleased with the overall response to Alba Palm Beach. We look forward to continued momentum as we approach the final phase of sales.” The joint venture completed the 22-story tower this year, having formed the condo association in April. The 1.2-acre development includes a private marina, a parking garage, and about 25,000 square feet dedicated to amenities. Kriss Capital, which is also serving as an administrative agent, added $36.6 million to the $19.9 million in outstanding debt from a construction loan that was boosted to $95 million in 2023. A representative for Kriss Capital did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The financing comes as West Palm Beach has seen a big rush of luxury condo development since the pandemic. At least 11 projects remain in the pipeline across the regional city with six under construction and another five having launched sales. These include Mast Capital’s Banyan Tree Residences, Terra’s Mr. C Residences, Related Ross’ South Flagler House and Shorecrest. Other projects have either been proposed or approved, including a second development from BGI Companies and Blue Road. The pair bought out the low-
bullets: BGI Companies and Blue Road secure $56.5M inventory loan (Kriss Capital) for Alba Palm Beach; 22 of 55 units unsold (40%).
55-unit waterfront condo tower, completed 2025, faces Intracoastal; development at stage requiring 'customary refinancing,' per developer.
High unsold inventory signals West Palm Beach luxury condo market softening or slower absorption.
stories.summary: BGI Companies and Blue Road obtained a $56.5 million inventory loan from Kriss Capital backing 22 unsold units (40% of total) in Alba Palm Beach, a newly completed 55-unit luxury waterfront condo tower on North Flagler Drive facing the Intracoastal Waterway, about 3 miles north of downtown West Palm Beach. The developer characterized the loan as a 'customary refinancing process' for condo projects at this stage and noted strong interest in remaining units.
stories.impact: Nearly 40% unsold units at completion in West Palm Beach luxury condos signals absorption slowdown and tightening buyer appetite in a formerly red-hot market; refinancing need (rather than outright sale) suggests developer patience on pricing or strategic pricing flexibility. This signals risk to future ultra-luxury condo development in South Florida; multifamily rental may outperform condo sales as investor capital rebalances toward income-producing assets. Monitor West Palm Beach absorption rates and pricing trends—if unsold inventory persists, builders may shift to rental or paused development.

stories.title: JBL scores approval for massive Deerfield Beach shopping center redev
stories.excerpt: Deerfield Beach greenlit a massive mixed-use redevelopment of the Rivertowne Square shopping center, paving the way for hundreds of residential units and thousands of square feet of commercial space. City commissioners unanimously approved a rezoning, site plan and development agreement Tuesday, allowing JBL Asset Management, led by Jacob Khotoveli, to move forward with redevelopment of the 13-acre property at 1015 to 1219 South Federal Highway.  The existing shopping center, built in 1980 and acquired by JBL for $18.7 million in 2022, is anchored by Winn Dixie and is about half occupied, according to its website.  Redevelopment plans call for a […]This article originally appeared on The Real Deal. Click here to read the full story.
bullets: Deerfield Beach unanimously approves JBL Asset Management's Rivertowne Square redevelopment: 736 apartments + 56,940 SF retail on 13-acre site.
JBL acquired center for $18.7M in 2022; existing 1980 property ~50% occupied; plan includes 106 affordable units (120% AMI), two eight-story buildings.
Mixed-use revitalization replaces underperforming retail anchor (Bealls); preserves Winn-Dixie, retains/relocates small-business tenants.
stories.summary: Deerfield Beach city commissioners unanimously approved a massive mixed-use redevelopment of Rivertowne Square shopping center by JBL Asset Management. The 13-acre project will demolish a Bealls building and replace it with two eight-story residential towers containing 736 apartments (116 studios, 379 one-bedrooms, 241 two-bedrooms), 106 of which are restricted to 120% AMI. The project retains and remodels the Winn-Dixie anchor and preserves 56,940 SF of retail, plus outparcels occupied by restaurants and service tenants. JBL acquired the property for $18.7 million in 2022 when the center was approximately 50% occupied.
stories.impact: Deerfield Beach's approval of large-scale retail-to-mixed-use conversion signals weak legacy retail demand in South Florida strip centers and developer confidence in rental (not condo) absorption as highest and best use. The 736-unit pipeline in Broward County adds meaningful supply; monitor lease-up and pricing relative to other Deerfield/Fort Lauderdale submarkets to gauge market velocity. This replicable playbook (underperforming 1980s center + affordable overlay) will likely accelerate conversions of similar-era retail stock across South Florida; developers should identify acquisition targets in 25–50% occupied centers with strong traffic patterns but poor merchandising/anchors.

stories.title: Elevating the Successful ‘Housing Is Health Care’ Model in New York
stories.excerpt: A recently released study confirmed — yet again — what members of the affordable housing community have repeatedly maintained: Housing is indeed health care. An analysis conducted for NYC Health + Hospitals’ Housing for Health initiative and MetroPlusHealth, an affordable health plan, found that in the two years after formerly homeless individuals were permanently housed, they experienced a 40 percent reduction in emergency room visits and a 36 percent reduction in inpatient hospital admissions. At the same time, preventative care visits among these tenants increased, as their housing stability gave them the time to more effectively manage their health. Carlina Rivera. Photo: Courtesy NYSASAF. The result was not just better health outcomes and improved living standards for the 250 formerly unhoused individuals who were placed in housing through this partnership, but also a significant Medicaid savings of $17,000 per person — a total of $3.2 million over two years. Added to a wealth of existing data on the link between housing and improved health — both physical and mental — this latest study underscores the importance of making smart, targeted investments that link services with safe, stable and high-quality housing as we continue to address the city’s affordable housing crisis. New York State Association for Affordable Housing (NYSAFAH) members have long recognized the importance of building developments that expand access to care. Two projects, both completed over the past year, exemplify best practices in this space, and were honored at NYSAFAH’s 2026 Awards for Excellence and Innovation event on Nov. 4. Willow Tree Commons, at 225 East 45th Street in Manhattan, received NYSAFAH’s Innovator of the Year award. It replaced a shelter that Project Renewal had run since 1998 in an outdated building that wasn’t originally designed for that purpose. That shelter was replaced with a new, 21-story building that combines permanent housing, emergency shelter, health care an
bullets: NYC Housing for Health initiative study: 250 formerly homeless individuals permanently housed; 40% ER visit reduction, 36% inpatient admission reduction.
$17K per-person Medicaid savings over 2 years ($3.2M total); preventative care visits increased; housing stability improved health outcomes.
Demonstrates housing-as-healthcare model; policy/financing implications for affordable multifamily development.
stories.summary: An analysis of NYC Health + Hospitals' Housing for Health initiative and MetroPlusHealth found that formerly homeless individuals who were permanently housed experienced a 40% reduction in emergency room visits and a 36% reduction in inpatient hospital admissions within two years. The study tracked 250 formerly unhoused individuals and documented $17,000 per-person Medicaid savings over two years, totaling $3.2 million, while preventative care visits increased as housing stability enabled better health management.
stories.impact: Housing-as-healthcare evidence strengthens the financial case for supportive multifamily development in NYC and nationally; Medicaid and health insurer co-investment in deeply affordable, supportive housing projects now has quantified ROI. Developers should engage healthcare systems (hospital networks, managed care organizations) as anchor tenants or co-capital sources for supportive housing; NYC's model may be replicated in other metros with high ER utilization and Medicaid enrollment. This creates a new capital source (healthcare entities) and financing rationale (healthcare cost offsets) for otherwise uneconomic deeply affordable projects.

stories.title: Kids Art Studio ColorPop Workshop to Open at Tribeca’s 450 Washington Street
stories.excerpt: A pop of color can certainly brighten your day. ColorPop Workshop, an art studio offering children ages 3 to 12 a variety of classes, has inked a 1,000-square-foot deal at the base of Related Companies’ 450 Washington Street in Manhattan’s Tribeca neighborhood, according to tenant broker Meridian Retail Leasing. “ColorPop started as a passion project. We built the studio we dreamed of, one that brings the incredible creative talent of New York City to kids: a working artist in every room, materials most kids never get to touch like resin, polymer clay, and plaster, and the excitement of new projects every single week,” a spokesperson for ColorPop said in a statement to Commercial Observer. “With studios on the Upper East Side and in the Hamptons, Tribeca is the perfect next stop, and we can’t wait to bring a little ColorPop magic downtown.” The length of the lease, which was signed Nov. 17, was not disclosed. The asking rent was $180 per square foot. Lindsay Zegans from Ripco Real Estate represented the landlord in the deal, while Meridian’s Max Freudenberger and Noam Aziz represented ColorPop Workshop. “ColorPop Workshop has built a loyal following with families uptown and in Southampton, and Tribeca was the natural next step,” Aziz said in a statement. ColorPop offers weekly two-hour workshops, open studio sessions, school summer camps and birthday parties. This will be the studio’s third Manhattan location alongside its spots at 1289 Madison Avenue and 135 East 63rd Street, both on the Upper East Side. “ColorPop is a perfect fit for Tribeca’s growing community of young families, giving kids a vibrant, creative studio right in their own neighborhood,” Zegans told CO. “We’re thrilled to have helped add them to Related’s retail at 450 Washington Street.” Spanning a full block on the Tribeca waterfront, 450 Washington Street is a 176-unit condominium building completed by Related in 2009. Retail activation at base of large mixed-use residential tower (Related development); lease signed Nov. 17; length not disclosed.
Tribeca retail leasing momentum; no multifamily development signal.
stories.summary: ColorPop Workshop, a children's art studio offering classes for ages 3–12, leased 1,000 square feet at the base of Related Companies' 450 Washington Street mixed-use residential tower in Manhattan's Tribeca neighborhood. The lease was signed November 17 at an asking rent of $180 per square foot. ColorPop operates studios on the Upper East Side and in the Hamptons.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. Ground-floor retail activation at Related's residential tower reflects strong Tribeca retail demand and mixed-use lease-up momentum but does not inform apartment development strategy or market conditions.

stories.title: “Unbearable”: How South Florida developers handle intense flooding
stories.excerpt: In Florida, when it rains, it pours. Not everyone is prepared for knee-high flood water or widespread power outages. But for contractors and developers, it’s part of the job. Historic rainfall, supercharged by El Niño and king tides climate events, has flooded parts of Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, along with other east coast cities.  Several counties declared states of emergencies this week, while Broward and Miami-Dade counties shut down schools and other public facilities. In Hollywood, a synagogue roof caved in under the rain, and some 70 residents of an apartment building were rescued from inundated units. bullets: South Florida (Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach) inundated with historic rainfall, king tides, flooding; states of emergency declared; construction delays expected.
Contractors employ generators, pumps, weather monitoring to mitigate flooding risk; delays and cost overruns 'unbearable,' per El-Ad CEO on $1B Davie mixed-use project.
Climate risk and infrastructure strain intensify development costs, timelines, insurance in South Florida; potential headwind to margin and delivery schedules.
stories.summary: Historic rainfall events supercharged by climate conditions flooded Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties, prompting emergency declarations, school closures, and widespread power outages. Contractors report use of generators and pumps to mitigate on-site risk, but flooding causes significant delays and cost escalations. El-Ad National Properties' CEO described delays as 'unbearable' for The Plaza at Davie, a $1 billion, 2.8 million-square-foot mixed-use project.
stories.impact: South Florida's intensifying flood risk raises hard costs (resilience infrastructure, elevated construction, insurance) and soft costs (permitting delays, project timelines) for multifamily development, compressing margins and extending hold periods. Insurance and lender scrutiny on climate/flood exposure will likely tighten financing terms and require elevated resilience capex (elevated structures, pumping systems, stormwater management). Developers should budget +5–10% for climate-resilience hardening and model rising insurance/property tax risk in pro formas for South Florida projects; this may favor inland sites or higher-elevation areas and slow velocity of waterfront/intracoastal development.

stories.title: CRE Positioned to Withstand 2022 Repeat Amid Rising Rates: NYU Schack Panelists
stories.excerpt: While the commercial real estate industry may be contending with multiple interest rate hikes in 2027, the industry is better equipped today to avoid market dislocation that occurred in 2022, according to debt investors at the 59th annual New York University Schack Institute of Real Estate Capital Markets conference. Unlike 2022, when financing sources were limited, CRE owners now have far more options to access capital through banks, insurance companies and private lenders, said Michael Wiebolt, global chief investment officer of Blackstone Real Estate Debt Strategies. The Federal Reserve began aggressively hiking interest rates starting in March 2022, resulting in valuation dips across a number of CRE properties and owners unable to gain new financing amid higher borrowing costs. “We went through a protracted period beginning in 2022 of pretty limited availability of debt capital,” said Wiebolt during the NYU conference’s global finance and capital markets panel held Thursday morning at the Pierre Hotel in Midtown Manhattan. “That’s a very different dynamic than we’re experiencing today” Wiebolt noted that another important distinction between 2022 and late 2026 is the oversupply dynamics that were at play then in certain asset classes. He said today construction activity has been down significantly in recent years, which should create a “tailwind for accelerating fundamental performance” that could offset some of the capital value impacts from rising interest rates. Another factor that should position the CRE market for near-term sustained higher borrowing costs is disciplined underwriting from lenders over the past few years, according to Mark Romanczuk, head of Americas CRE finance at Goldman Sachs. bullets: NYU Schack panel: CRE debt markets better positioned vs. 2022 despite potential 2027 rate hikes; capital sources diversified (banks, insurance, private lenders).
Blackstone's Wiebolt notes 2022 saw 'protracted period of limited debt capital availability'; today's multi-source environment reduces refinance/acquisition financing risk.
Industry consensus: improved resilience to interest rate shocks; lower likelihood of 2022-style liquidity crisis and distress.
stories.summary: Debt investors at NYU Schack Institute's 59th annual Capital Markets conference indicated that the commercial real estate industry is better positioned to withstand potential 2027 interest rate hikes compared to the dislocation experienced in 2022. Michael Wiebolt of Blackstone noted that unlike 2022—when financing sources were scarce—today's CRE debt market offers multiple capital pathways through banks, insurance companies, and private lenders, reducing refinance and acquisition risk.
stories.impact: Diversified debt markets lower refinancing risk for multifamily developers but do not eliminate rate and valuation pressure if 2027 brings additional Fed tightening. Capital availability remains rate-sensitive; higher rates will compress cap rates and valuations, but widespread lender exit (as in 2022) is less likely. For developers, this means: (1) rate-lock mezzanine and permanent debt now while spreads remain relatively favorable; (2) refinance near-term maturities (2026–2027) ahead of potential tightening; (3) assume higher carry costs in pro formas. The improved capital environment does not guarantee favorable terms—only that liquidity won't evaporate entirely.
